changes.title: Tool removed: mcp__terminal__run_in_terminal

before.description: Type a shell command into a tab of the user's Terminal panel (beside this conversation) and press Enter. The command runs in the user's interactive login shell (zsh, bash or sh, with their aliases, PATH and credentials) — on their computer, or on the SSH host in an SSH session — outside any sandbox, stays running after your turn ends, and its tab is added without opening the panel: the user can open the panel to watch it, type into it and stop it with Ctrl-C; you stop it, or close its tab when you are done with it, with stop_terminal_tab. Returns the tab's tab_id once the command is typed, which waits for the shell's startup files to finish (usually at once, longer for a slow shell); read what it printed with read_terminal {tab_id, wait_for_output_ms}. Prefer this over Bash for long-running or interactive things the user should see and control — dev servers, file watchers, test runners in watch mode, log tails, REPLs — and over preview_start for processes that are not an HTTP server to preview. Use Bash for short commands whose output you need in this turn. With no tab_id a call opens a new tab in cwd (default the session's working directory). Do not open a tab per command: to run the next command, pass the tab_id of a tab you opened earlier whose shell is back at its prompt (list_terminal_tabs marks it reusable: true), and keep new tabs for things that keep running, like a dev server or a watcher. A reused tab is the same shell as before, so its directory, aliases and variables are wherever earlier commands left them, the output of earlier commands stays above the new output, and cwd cannot be combined with tab_id. Give each tab you open its own short title of letters, digits, spaces and . _ , & + : # / ' -: the approval card names the tab, so one whose name is missing, uses other characters or reads the same as another tab's cannot be reused, and one renamed before the user answers is refused (ask again with the names list_terminal_tabs shows). `command` is one complete command line in printable ASCII, as you would type it at the prompt: pipelines, && / || / ;, quotes, variables, redirections and subshells are all fine. before.description: Send Ctrl-C to a Terminal-panel tab you opened (with run_in_terminal or open_terminal_tab) to stop what is running in it, or with close: true close the tab, which ends whatever runs in it. Use it to stop a dev server, watcher or other long-running command you started once it is no longer needed, and to close your finished tabs so they do not pile up, instead of asking the user to. It acts only on tabs you opened in this session that the user has not typed in, never on one the user opened, and types no command. changes.title: New setting: disableReplyCheck

after.description: Disable the reply check in Claude Tag sessions on a self-hosted runner. The check re-prompts Claude, at most four times a turn, when a turn ends without a call to one of Claude Tag's reply tools. It is not a hook, so disableAllHooks does not affect it. Disabling it also stops two messages to Claude that Anthropic's service can request for such a session: a nudge after a long stretch of work with no visible update, and a reminder added to prompts. Claude Code's built-in reminder to give progress updates, on models that have it, is then no longer held back. Set it in managed settings; false there keeps the check on. Everywhere else it is ignored and the check stays on. Has no effect on sessions that Anthropic hosts.

changes.title: New setting: disableWindowsBashCommandSplit

after.description: Windows only. Set to true to keep every Bash command in a single argument to bash, so that endpoint security tools that match text in process command lines see it whole. Otherwise Claude Code may split a long command over several arguments. With true, a command of about 7,000 characters or more, or fewer if it is full of quotes, may reach bash cut short, and then usually fails with a syntax error. Only honored from managed settings; ignored in user, project, local and --settings sources.
